opus-5.5.text:
I think Latour is really helpful here because he pushes back on two very tempting pictures we often have of technology. One is the instrumentalist view, the idea that a tool is just a neutral means, and all the moral significance lies with the person who wields it. The classic slogan is "guns don't kill people, people kill people." The other is a kind of technological determinism, where the artifact itself drives outcomes regardless of what humans intend.

What Latour does is reject both of those in favor of something more relational. In his discussion of the gun example, he says that neither the person nor the gun alone is the relevant actor. Instead you get a new hybrid agent, the person-with-a-gun, and that combined entity has different goals, capacities and dispositions than either component on its own. The person who picks up a gun is, in a meaningful sense, a different actor than they were before. So the artifact isn't passive; it mediates action. It translates intentions, it opens up some possibilities and closes off others.

He has lovely, quite mundane examples of this: the speed bump, which he calls a "sleeping policeman," or the hotel key with a heavy weight attached so guests remember to return it. In each case a moral or social norm, "drive slowly," "return the key," has been delegated to a material object. The script is literally built into the thing. And once you see that, it becomes very hard to maintain that technology is value neutral, because values are being inscribed into artifacts all the time, sometimes deliberately and sometimes without anyone quite noticing.

For me, that lens is especially important for thinking about AI. These systems aren't just neutral conduits for whatever a user wants to do. Design choices about what a model will or won't do, how it frames information, what it defaults to, all embed particular judgments about what matters. And as AI systems become more agentic and more woven into people's lives, that mediating role becomes more pronounced. So the question isn't whether values are present in the technology; they inevitably are. The question is which values, whose values, and through what process they get there. That's what pushes us toward questions of legitimacy, of fair processes for deciding on the principles these systems embody, rather than pretending we can stay neutral by simply building tools and stepping back.

r001.rationale: The response says artifacts mediate action by opening some possibilities and closing others, and uses this to challenge technology’s value neutrality.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that introducing a technology makes returning to a world without it difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think Latour is useful here precisely because he refuses to let us draw the line we usually want to draw, between the thing itself and the uses people make of it. The standard neutrality view says a hammer is just a hammer; whether it builds a house or breaks a window is entirely down to the person holding it. Latour's move is to say that this picture systematically misdescribes what's actually going on.

His famous example is the speed bump, or what he calls the "sleeping policeman." A municipality wants drivers to slow down near a school. It could post a sign appealing to their sense of civic responsibility. Instead it pours a lump of concrete into the road. Now the driver slows down not out of concern for children but out of concern for their suspension. What's happened is that a moral injunction, "drive carefully," has been delegated to an object. The value hasn't disappeared; it's been translated into a different material and now operates through the artefact rather than through persuasion. Latour's point is that the artefact is doing normative work. It's enforcing a rule, distributing responsibility, shaping what's easy and hard to do.

So on this view, technologies are better understood as participants in networks of human and non-human actors, each of which carries what he calls "scripts" or "programs of action." A door closer, a seatbelt that won't let the car start, a turnstile: these all encode a particular settlement about how people ought to behave, and they enforce it with a stubbornness that a human enforcer often lacks. The values are built in at the level of design, often invisibly, and they persist long after the designers have moved on.

Where I find this especially relevant for AI is that it undercuts the move of saying the model is just a tool and all the ethical questions live downstream with the deployer or the user. Latour would say that's a kind of mystification. When you decide what a system optimises for, what data it learns from, what it refuses to do, which users it's designed around, you're writing scripts into the artefact. Those choices will shape conduct at scale, and they're political in his sense whether or not anyone intended them to be.

Now, I'd add a caveat, because I think Latour can be read in an overly deflationary way. The framework is very good at showing that values are present in technology. It's less good, on its own, at telling us which values ought to be there. Latour was somewhat allergic to normative theory in the traditional sense. So I tend to treat him as diagnostic. He helps us see that the neutrality thesis is a kind of alibi, a way of escaping responsibility for the settlements we're embedding into things. But once you accept that, you still face the properly ethical and political question of how those settlements should be arrived at, and who gets a say. That's where I think work on alignment and value pluralism has to pick up where the sociology of technology leaves off.

r001.rationale: It says technologies encode scripts that shape conduct and make some actions easier or harder, challenging the view that they are neutral.

r002.rationale: It says embedded values persist after designers move on, but does not state that introducing technology makes it difficult to return to a world without it.

astra-6.text:
I think Latour challenges that idea by showing how values become embedded in the things we build. Technology doesn’t simply sit there, waiting for someone to decide whether to use it well or badly. Its design helps shape what people do, which choices are available to them, and which choices are easy or difficult.

Take a speed bump. You can ask drivers to slow down because they have a responsibility to pedestrians, or you can build something into the road that makes them slow down. In that second case, you’ve delegated part of the work of enforcing a norm to a material object. The speed bump isn’t morally responsible, but it’s also not neutral with respect to how people behave.

So the challenge is to look beyond the intentions of the individual user and ask how values are expressed through the whole arrangement of people and technologies. For AI, that means asking not just what someone does with a system, but what forms of behaviour and relationships the system itself encourages.

r001.rationale: The candidate says technology design shapes what people do, which choices are available, and which are easy or difficult, explaining why technology is not value neutral.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say that introducing a technology makes returning to a world without it difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Latour challenges the picture in which technology is simply a passive instrument, with all the values coming from the person who uses it. On his account, artifacts help shape what we do. They make some actions easier, make others harder, and sometimes take over roles that would otherwise be performed by people.

Take a speed bump. You could ask drivers to slow down out of concern for pedestrians, or you could build something into the road that makes them slow down. In that second case, a particular prescription for behavior has been delegated to an artifact. The driver might respond out of concern for their suspension rather than concern for pedestrians, but the design still helps produce a particular social outcome.

So the challenge to value neutrality is that technologies don’t just transmit our intentions unchanged. Their design helps organize our choices and relationships. That doesn’t mean an artifact has intentions in the human sense, but it does mean that understanding its ethical significance requires looking at how it participates in shaping action.

r001.rationale: The response says artifacts shape what people do and that design organizes choices and relationships, making technology more than a value-neutral instrument.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that introducing technology makes it difficult to return to a world without it.
